slides.title: A signal is a value indexed by time
slides.lead: Axes, units and timestamps are part of the data.
points: t_s is seconds; ax, ay, az are m/s²
gx, gy, gz are angular velocity in rad/s
100 rows at 50 Hz cover a nominal 2 s window; last timestamp is 1.98 s
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Accelerometer and gyroscope
slides.lead: An accelerometer at rest measures about 1 g; a gyro measures rotation rate.
points: Tilting redistributes gravity among acceleration axes
A stationary gyro is near zero plus noise and bias
Acceleration alone cannot separate gravity from dynamic acceleration
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Gravity and magnitude
points: Changing orientation keeps the static magnitude near 9.80665 m/s²
Dynamic acceleration can raise or lower it
A magnitude near 1 g alone does not prove the board is still
slides.notes: Use the tilt slider without added acceleration, then add acceleration. Constant velocity also leaves the accelerometer near 1 g.

slides.title: Read a NumPy array by its shape
slides.lead: acc is N × 3; the magnitude is a length-N array.
points: acc ** 2 squares every element
sum(axis=1) adds the three axes within each row
sqrt takes the square root of each sum
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Sampling turns a curve into measurements
slides.lead: At 50 Hz, the nominal sample period is 20 ms.
points: Ts = 1/fs; samples do not contain everything between timestamps
Try reducing fs while keeping the signal frequency fixed
Connect the orange dots to the sampling rate, not the canvas refresh rate
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Estimate the actual rate
slides.lead: Use the timestamps rather than assuming a loop runs exactly on schedule.
points: diff(t) gives N−1 time gaps
median resists a few long gaps better than mean
1 / median gap estimates the dominant sampling rate
Inspect lost counts too: median can hide occasional missing samples
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Find the gravity axis
slides.lead: Take each axis mean, then find the largest absolute component.
points: mean(axis=0) averages each column
abs handles screen-up and screen-down signs
argmax returns an index, not the acceleration itself
This interpretation needs a mostly still window
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Read the repository’s four motions
slides.lead: These curves come from the exact bundled CSV rows.
points: Select idle, shake, circle or lift and compare all acceleration axes
The files are synthetic examples with sensor-like noise
They are useful for repeatability; they do not measure a student’s motion
slides.notes: Have students find the active axes before selecting the next gesture. Use the gyro view too; later the model uses all six channels.

slides.title: Noise is meaningful only in context
slides.lead: Lab 9.1 prints standard deviations over its first second.
points: Begin live recording by holding the board still
In default replay, idle comes first
A moving first second produces motion variation, not a sensor noise estimate
Compare axis units and scale before calling one signal noisier
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Lost samples leave timestamp gaps
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

quiz.explanation: 1.060 and 1.080 s are missing. USB load, slow processing or resets can disrupt acquisition; replay reports lost=0.

slides.title: Run Lab 9.1 and explain the plot
slides.lead: Predict the stationary magnitude before pressing Enter.
points: Replay: the default 8 s takes four 100-row files once
Live: move, then hold still; inspect samples, rate and lost
Lift: acceleration and braking change the magnitude around gravity
Compare individual axes with magnitude; keep their different meanings clear
slides.notes: Ask for three pieces of evidence: sample period, gravity magnitude and one motion feature. Do not accept “it looks right” alone.

slides.title: Checkpoint: magnitude is not a motion oracle
points: This is consistent with a tilted stationary board
It does not exclude constant velocity or every possible dynamic motion
Check the gyro and the time history to strengthen your conclusion
slides.notes: The checkpoint’s intended answer is a still tilted board. Explain the physical limit without turning a useful rule of thumb into an absolute test.
